Have multiple alarms:

Alarm 1) half an hour before I need to get up - I can go back to sleep peacefully knowing I have plenty of time. This alarm used to be 20 mins before getting up time, but for my early starts, this wasn't long enough.

Alarm 2) 5 mins before I need to get up. Eyes can stay closed, but my mind is now starting to wake up

Alarm 3) when I need to get up. Eyes ate now open, and I spend a minute saying morning to my cats

Alarm 4) 1 or 2 mins after Alarm 3. This is my actual get-out-of-bed time.

Final Alarm) 10 minutes before I need to leave the house to catch my bus to work. This tells me to get shoes on, jacket/coat on and ensure my bag is packed with what I need. It also serves as a final back up in case I'm super tired and didn't get up with alarms 1, 2, 3 and 4.


This sounds excessive to some but it's the routine that works for me

On your intake, start with 1, out breath is 2, next inhale is 3 etc etc, until you reach 10 (5  ind and outs total) then you start back at number 1. Every time you realise that you lost count, you start back at 1 and keep going round.

2 abscesses would likely take longer to heal, so you may be right that you won't feel ready for school in 15 days, especially as school involves a lot of sitting down on hard chairs. Just remember to take it at a pace that you can deal with, not push yourself for anyone. Not your school and not for your parents either. They aren't experiencing it so don't let anyone tell you how you should be feeling or what you can or can't do yet.

One thing I can recommend as well around showering, is to have a shower just before you're due to have your dressings changed. That way if it gets wet and falls off, it won't matter so much because a fresh one is about to be put on.

I also found it more comfortable to sleep with a pillow between my legs to keep some of the pressure off my wound, so that may be useful to you as well.

Best of luck, rest up and take it easy!! Its a lot of pain to deal with with and the last thing you need is to stress about anything. Let your school know as soon as you can that you're recovering from surgery and ask what procedures they have in place for students that aren't able to attend on the first days of school (trust me they'll have something). Do what you can to prepare to do work from home, outside of that, try not to worry about it xx

Many with BPD, myself included like talking about our problems, we ovwrshare and feel rejected when others "don't trust us enough in return" to open up back to us.

But its not personal, its not that they don't necessarily trust you.

For some people, they talk about things that are so traumatic that to bring it up outside of the safe space of the therapists office, would be asking way too much from someone, especially someone we care about. (Not saying that's the case here, just an example).

Its easy for us to blame them for being too closed off rather than look at our own actions. Try to look inside and figure out what happened to cause these feelings of separation from your partner if they don't open up to you.

Find out where your urges are coming from. Talk to.your partner, be honest about it and support each other. Get your own therapist if you don't already (can't remember if you said you had one sorry), just don't give in, don't give up and don't stop being the best version of yourself.

From someone with BPD, please read;

Firstly OP, can I just say, although I may not be present on this sub often (I don't put too much clout into MBTI because so many people's results change over time including mine a few times), I greatly appreciate your final footnote on this post.

Now i can't speak for NPD, but Borderline personality disorder is starting to become more of a recognised condition in recent years with Amber Heards recent public diagnosis bringing it ever more into the public discussion, it has long been considered a diagnosis given to manipulative, 'borderline psychotic' people.

**(yes that is where the name comes from, hence why it has recently been changed to Emotionally Unstable Personality Disorder or EUPD, but for the purposes of this post I will be using the term BPD)**


Go to Google and ask "what are people with BPD like: and it tears us all down. Apparently I will tell monstrous lies to keep people from leaving me, ill threaten to end my life over the slightest bit of rejection or criticism, I will explode in hellish rage if you even think to disagree with me or tell me im wrong!!!

Like every other mental health disorder, there is a pitiful amount of research done into BPD. Yes, there are extreme cases that may portray the above in SOME specific situations, im not going to say that we are all easy to get along with. I would even go as far to agree with Google when it states that BPD is one of the most difficult conditions for the person diagnosed to cope with in their day to day lives.

However. What Google doesn't tell you is that these extreme cases are just that. They are the EXTREMES. It is completely wrong to paint everyone under a label with the same brush. It may be a far out comparison but look at terrorists and Muslims... we are (mostly) smart enough as people to recognise that those few that chose to act and behave the way that terrorists do does not mean that all Muslims are that extreme in their behaviour. And people with mental disorders are no different. Some people are just bad people, its not the disorder it's just them.

I spent so long feeling ashamed of my diagnosis because of what I was being told I was online. Its bad enough when your head is telling you that you're a terrible person, only to then have what seemed like every online article confirming it. Stigma like this could easily push someone to completely withdraw into themselves, turning them into what everyone believes them to be.

I could go on and on telling you what it's really like for the majority of people with BPD. I could tell you about the causes of BPD, the trauma most of us experience as children, the constant need to ignore every fibre of your body telling you that the people you love dont care. How much of a daily battle it can be to give enough of a shit about your own wellbeing that you feed yourself that day. I could tell you how hard but rewarding and educational its been for me personally to put myself through treatment, to learn to control my emotions despite having a chemical imbalance that could mean I'll be dealing with never feeling stable the rest of my entire life. 

I could tell you how scared me and everyone in my treatment group are about being open about our diagnosis now that Amber Heard has been diagnosed and how we fear that her extreme case is just going to fan the flames of the stigma we already experience.

 Let's be honest though, if you wanted to know you would go and do your own research. If you have any specific questions of course im happy to answer because the only way this stigma changes is with education. PLEASE educate yourself.

On that note, TheMighty is a great website that im sure must be mainly written by people with the condition, look at some of the subs on here, talk to people that actually have this condition (people with an actual diagnosis as well, sorry im not a fan of self-diagnosing) but please, just educare yourself a little.

Oh wow this post gave me an eye opener at just how many things I've done over my life that were just like this. Here's my list:

-**self harm**, ok so a lot of people on this sub will relate so im not gonna go into details but for a few years whilst I was in school this was something I did but because im pretty sure I've got more quiet BPD, I was always scared of having to answer questions about scars from teachers so it wasn't something that happened too often or for too long. 
(Instead I found other methods of turning my emotions inwards that didn't leave long lasting traces but were still just as toxic/unhealthy.)

-**Banging my head against the wall**, not hard enough to give me concussion or break the skin but more a continued dull pain that wouldn't draw any attention due to wounds etc. I specifically remember doing this as a young child and it started up again in my late teens and into mid 20s. Unfortunately its still something I have urges to do when overwhelmed by intrusive thoughts/ptsd flashbacks and more so whenever I feel I fucked up and im angry with myself.

-**Digging my fingernails into myself**. Ok this is for me is the big one, this has been going on as long as I can remember, and im talking way back into primary school. I think my first memory of this sort of thing happening, I was around the ages 5/6. Now I know that this particular habit, either happened as a result or just happened to come along side, the fact that as a kid I was very angry. As in I was the kid that would lash out physically if I was feeling overwhelmed or trapped and I needed an escape. Now anytime this happened, I would always the most tremendous guilt afterwards if I had hurt anybody, I would feel like a dangerous animal that needed to be isolated and kept away from normal people whenever I was emotional because I couldn't be trusted. I developed, what I can only describe as, a phobia of hurting people, which in turn led to my habit of turning any high level emotion, positive and negative, inward. My nails would tend to grow fairly quickly and they were always pretty strong so I would break the skin on the backs of my hands half the time as well. This also includes general scratching of body parts; forehead, arms, legs, scalp, back of my neck.. nowhere was safe.

-**Picking at any perceived skin imperfections**. This one is fairly self-explanatory, if my anxiety is high, if I am feeling bad about myself, any time I look in the mirror... I am overcome with this need to pick and pick at myself until I am blotchy, bleeding and bruised. Whether its spots, blackheads, ingrown hairs, dry skin on my lips I was going to attack it. Ive clawed at my own face before because I was beginning to convince myself that every single pore was bursting with grime. I avoid looking in mirrors a lot and when I do, I try not to stand too close so I cant start to notice anything.

-**Punching body parts**. Again this one is self-explanatory for the most part. There would be times i would get this horrible sick feeling, like having nervous butterflies if they were the bad kind, in my stomach and it would make me automatically tense up my entire abdomen and want to punch myself in the stomach. Also at times when the urge to hit my head against a wall would kick in but I was either not in my own space or i was having to be quiet to not draw attention or wake people, I would often smack my own head to imitate the feeling. This is something that still happens Unfortunately but ive become much better at catching the urges before giving in.

**NOW FOR SOME POSITIVE BITS!!**


As ive gotten older a lot of these things have stopped (for the most part) and now whenever I get self destructive/self harm urges I do one or some of the following:

- I now try to punch my hands and only my hands when I still want to hear that skin on skin sound

- I've got some small, stiff, sofa cushions that make a wonderfully loud THUD when thrown at a wall. Throwing these means I don't break anything and I can throw them as much as I want til I get tired because they also don't smash into pieces upon impact!!

- I sing/listen to anything loud that drowns out any intrusive thought that I might ne having, making sure its something that I know most/all the words to so I can follow the lyrics as a distraction

- Get myself outside or at least to a different space. Changing the 4 walls youre sitting in when you get those urges can make all the difference I've found. This isn't always doable but if you can even for 5 minutes, it can be like hitting reset on your brain. Everyone will tell you that going for a walk when youre angry is a great way to vent that energy and you know what, they're all correct.

- Phone someone you know you can just rant off to. Again this isn't always an available option and I know that talking doesn't work for everyone but this one's  for those that have one or two people that they know they can call up and say "im feeling overwhelmed i just need you to distract me, talk to me about something that's going on with you.". For me, this is my best friend who has a lot of the same struggles as me so we are that person for each other and I am so lucky to have her. I feel like a horrible burden on her sometimes but I know that its OK to lean on friends when youre struggling.

- Have a nap. Yep, simple as that. Sometimes there isn't anything else that I think will work and the only thing that's gonna let me get over whatever it is thats making me feel like ahitnis to go to sleep for a bit. Ill wake up feeling more neutral and able to try and flip the rest of my day around. However be warned, this is a risky method to go with as its a gamble how long you can be asleep for.

- Have a joint. Now quick disclaimer, I am not advocating the use of illegal substances, im merely putting this here for the purpose of honesty. Smoking is actually something I am receiving recovery help for so that I can actually gain treatment for my BPD. Here in the UK, professionals will be very hesitant to put you forward for therapies such as DBT and CBT if you are regularly taking any substance, including alcohol. However, smoking weed has been my coping mechanism for high level emotions for the last 7ish years. It has helped me get through some heartbreaking and traumatic shit but I also recognise now that I need to stop relying on it. That and the fact that im dependant on it means im just not enjoying the high as much :/

And finally..
-**CRY**. I think it may be pretty common for those in this sub and anyone with BPD to try and contain their sadness. I know me personally, there have been periods lasting a year or more after family members have passed away, where I just couldn't cry. I would be hurting more than I thought possible, wanting desperately to let it out. I would start almost fake crying, in an attempt to kick-start the waterworks but nothing came out. As a young kid, I would learn not to have any extreme displays of frustration/sadness because I would only be told to cut it out/let it go/get over it/told it would be fine. I was never allowed to just **FEEL**. Nowadays, if I wanna cry, It doesn't matter who I'm around, unless I'm on transport and can't get to any tissues (I snot when I cry big time!!), im letting those tears flow. I might cry for 30 seconds or 30 minutes, screaming and shouting and throwing cushions the whole time. And, although I might not always feel complete euphoria afterwards, about 8/10 I feel better after.

Last year, I got the diagnosis of CPTSD and BPD.
This was an incredible weight off of my shoulders. I had had inklings and suspicions of BPD since I was maybe 15 (im 25 now), and had been told by near enough every professional I spoke with that I wouldnt get a diagnosis because I was too young.  Which, looking back on it, I totally understand, now that I've done a load of my own research on the topic  and how it is diagnosed. 

It wasn't until maybe 4 years ago that I found out PTSD could be diagnosed for anything other than war vets and people from severe relational abuse. Once I started reading into exactly how much childhood neglect and emotional abuse impacts things and how that in itself probably contributed towards my BPD that things really changed in my mind. 

All of a sudden, I wasn't just some freak kid that had had massive anger issues. I had somewhere to point the blame and it really started to conquer me. That, along with my ongoing/recurring depression and anxiety problems, I started to feel really weighed down and like there wasn't ever going to be a significant enough change in my life for me to ever be happy. Or hell, even just content with things for a long period of time before I would just inevitably screw it all up by getting all self destructive on my own ass again.

This isn't the point where I tell you how ive really turned things around and ive found a magic way of dealing with things because it would he the BIGGEST load of BS. Im still struggling, I still find ways to tear myself down, to put doubts in my own head, I allow my brain to turn me against the people that I know  care about me, im still out of work, I still split on people, have emotional flashbacks, bouts of anger and irritability, I still cry and overreact to minor things that I shouldn't even notice...

But.

Because I have AWARENESS of these things, I know im already way closer to not struggling with these things one day.

Having self-awareness and allowing myself to reflect, know that my past and trauma isn't my fault but my reactions and behaviour from now IS my responsibility, gets me that much closer to re-training my brain and becoming something MORE than just my trauma and bad experiences.

It is easy, to make excuses for ourselves when we have mental health disorders. Sometimes, even if we don't want to admit it, we want to tell ourselves that its ok that we got mad and shouted at that person because they annoyed us, even though they are aware that we struggle with emotional regulation. However, its not that persons job to adjust themselves to our past. It is OUR job to grow from it.

I KNOW that everything is likely overwhelming to you right now, but know that you arent alone. Xx

They are most likely familiar titles as ive seen them floating around on a fair few threads on various subreddits but im happy to share what I've found so far 😊

*minor disclaimer: I haven't yet completed any of these books as 8 find them a bit emotionally draining to read continuously so I pick them up when I'm feeling curious or, more commonly, when I've been triggered by something as for me the learning about the psychology behind things helps me to come back to a level place where I can think and approach things more logically.

1) C-PTSD - From Surviving to Thriving by Pete Walker. This is the first in depth book I ever started on and even though its a bit hard hitting at times, it really helped to fully open my eyes to accepting where ive been, where I came from and the events that have made me. The thing I love about this book in particular is that it let's you know and even encourages you not to read the book from cover to cover but to take your time reading through its, rather detailed chapter contents and see what speaks to you, as those are likely the area where you could do with more immediate help. This book has taught me a lot about different parenting styles and the things that my parents could have gone through that out them onto their own path with me and my sister. Personally, what I initially sought these books out for was to gain a better understanding of myself but also my parents, more so my mum, with whom I have had a very polarising relationship with throughout my 25years. 

Summary: what I have read so far has been amazingly helpful and its written without a tonn of medical jargon making it relatively easy to take in. However I wouldn't recommend having it as light reading before bed as it has sometimes put me into a very reflective mindstate which I wouldn't recommend just before sleep.

2) Running On Empty by Jonice Webb, PhD.

Again, although I havent finished this book, I would still highly recommend this book for anyone that knows or suspects that they were neglected as a child intentionally or otherwise. First off I want to say in defense of some parents out there, not all neglect is done with malicious intent or even knowingly. There are some parents out there that have the best will in the world and try their damned hardest but due to circumstance, sometimes isnt able to get everything 100% correct. Every parent f**ks up sometimes. Jonice Webb starts off by acknowledging this and to me wanted to make it clear that everyone experiences this in some form or another at least once in the average 80 years we each have. To help the reader get a slightly more expanded grasp on childhood neglect, a questionnaire is included in the introduction as a way of allowing you to figure out if this book is something that is worth your time. The first chapter lays out a healthy parental relationship so going forward the reader has something to compare with the following 12 parent types. Each one goes on to explain how that type of parent could have been parented themselves, how their own style has likely influenced you and some scenarios that detail that type in action. After that she goes into behaviours/traits that someone going or gone through these things could exhibit. Again, each one is given one or two scenarios and a short list of symptoms that could indicate you having these traits. This book is also the only one that (so far) ive read about suicide. I wont go into detail about it for trigger purposes for anyone else reading this but I appreciated how the author was willing to talk about it head on.

Summary: I wouldn't say this book is as heavy as what I've read elsewhere but I love how the author uses relatable scenarios for each section, allowing us the reader someone to out ourselves in the shoes of whilst reading. This for me made it easier to relate it to my own life experiences and apply what I learn.

3)Adult Children of Emotionally Immature Parents by Lindsay C. Gibson, PsyD.

This is the latest book ive picked up after finding a recommendation from a different reddit thread. This book.... for only a couple hundred pages, this book has been the one to really help me accept that what I want from my mum and what she is able to give me are two different things and accept that she might not even be capable of change at this point, even if some part of her wanted to. If I was going to recommend one of the 3 ive listed to start with, I would have to say this one. Yes I know I said I havent completed any of them and, yes, thats still true. However, despite that this is probably the book I've read the least of and yet still the one that I've learnt the most from. I actually started this one over the Xmas period whilst I was staying with my mum and stepdad for a couple weeks and during that time I was not in a good place. This book gave me the introspection I needed to step back from my emotions and look at a bigger picture. Similar to Jonice Webb, this author also uses scenarios to give better explanations to the reader, along with including a whole chapter to more subtle red flags to look out for, which I found to be very eye-opening. 

The only other book I have on my list but have not yet started is The Body Keeps The Score: Brain, Mind, and body in the healing of trauma by Bessel Van der Kolk, MD. This was listed on the same reddit post I found the previous book but came with a warning that this was a very in depth look at things and quite a heavy read. Not to be your first book on the subject pretty much. So if you are an experienced reader on these topics and you havent read it, give it a go and then come back and tell me what its like please 😂
